title: Thunder scene (lines 1502–1605)

teacherSummary.text: Thunder sounds. Oedipus knows his end has come and calls for Theseus. Without a guide, he leads Theseus and his daughters toward the place of his passing, and tells Theseus that the secret, passed from ruler to heir, will protect Athens.

items.expected: Each question pulls a next fact into the open and keeps the audience with her. She first asks why Theseus is wanted at all; her father answers that the winged peal must bear him to Hades, and that they must send without delay. “And wherefore, father, dost thou summon him?” (line 1515). She then asks what sign convinces him, and later what solemn charge he would impress on the prince. “How knowest thou? items.prompt: Analyze “This winged thunder of the god must bear me / Anon to Hades”. What does Oedipus claim, and how should those words be taught?
items.expected: He claims that the peal is the god's, that it has wings, and that it must carry him soon to Hades; the next words tell them to send and not delay. “This winged thunder of the god must bear me / Anon to Hades. Send and tarry not.” (lines 1516–1517). “Winged” and “must bear me” make the sign an escort, and “Anon” marks the time as near. The lines should be taught as a god-sent summons, accepted in this scene: a natural end named by the man it concerns. They also explain, in the same breath, why Theseus must be called at once.

He first treats the din as a storm, then, trusting a true prophet, asks what must be done

Each question pulls a next fact into the open and keeps the audience with her. She first asks why Theseus is wanted at all; her father answers that the winged peal must bear him to Hades, and that they must send without delay. “And wherefore, father, dost thou summon him?” (line 1515). She then asks what sign convinces him, and later what solemn charge he would impress on the prince. “How knowest thou? What sign convinces thee?” (line 1527). “What solemn charge would’st thou impress on him?” (line 1540). The questions do not invent the summons; they pace it, so that the need for Theseus, the ground of certainty, and the promised charge are named before the king himself is on stage.

He claims that the peal is the god's, that it has wings, and that it must carry him soon to Hades; the next words tell them to send and not delay. “This winged thunder of the god must bear me / Anon to Hades. Send and tarry not.” (lines 1516–1517). “Winged” and “must bear me” make the sign an escort, and “Anon” marks the time as near. The lines should be taught as a god-sent summons, accepted in this scene: a natural end named by the man it concerns. They also explain, in the same breath, why Theseus must be called at once.

For much of the play other people have had to lead him; here he says he will take Theseus to the spot himself, without a guiding hand. “Myself anon without a guiding hand / Will take thee to the spot where I must end.” (lines 1570–1571). The reversal is not a recovery of ordinary eyesight, and it is not a boast that he has chosen the fact of the end. It shows that the summons gives him a path he can walk, and a charge he can place in Theseus's keeping, at the place appointed in this land. He leads because he is being led by the sign and by the god, and the seeing king must now follow the blind man who knows the way.

The last words are not a lament and not a report of an accomplished end; they are a blessing and a civic charge. He blesses his dearest friend, the land, and its followers, and he asks that, in their prosperity, they still think of him, when he is dead, for their welfare. That turn toward the city's good matches the gift he has just placed in Theseus's care. The written exit names Theseus followed by Antigone and Ismene; by the sense of his own command to follow, he leads them as they go. The scene stops there. It does not describe a later report of the end, and it does not tell us what will later be refused or where the daughters will next be sent.

Whom ye have led so long should lead you now.

items.text: Why does Oedipus no longer need a guide?
items.lookFor: He is led by the god, and his inner sight now guides him: the blind man who was led all play becomes the leader of the sighted.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Oedipus says, “Myself anon without a guiding hand / Will take thee to the spot where I must end” (lines 1570–1571), and he names the god who leads him: “For this way Hermes leads, the spirit guide” (line 1597). The reversal is striking: “Strange that I / Whom ye have led so long should lead you now” (lines 1592–1593). The blind man is guided by the gods, so he no longer needs a human guide.

items.text: What does “Thunder scene (lines 1502–1605)” suggest about the summons? State the inference and the line that supports it.
items.lookFor: Oedipus recognises the peals as the gods’ appointed warning and sends for Theseus while he can still speak the charge.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Oedipus reads the peals as the sign he was promised: “The gods themselves are heralds of my fate; / Of their appointed warnings nothing fails” (lines 1561–1562). His first thought is not fear but his promise to his host: he asks whether Theseus will “Find me yet living and my senses clear” (line 1539). The scene suggests that he meets the summons calmly and as a man keeping faith.

items.text: Find one example of plot in “Thunder scene (lines 1502–1605)”. What does it reveal about the summons that a plain statement would not?
items.lookFor: A plot example, such as the blind man leading the sighted, explained for what it reveals: the summons gives Oedipus authority and certainty he has lacked all play.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The blind man now leads: “Follow me, daughters, this way” (line 1592). This plot reversal shows more than a plain statement could. All play Oedipus has been led, seated, moved and argued over; the summons gives him the certainty and authority to lead the people who have guided him.

items.text: How does the irony in “Thunder scene (lines 1502–1605)” shape what we understand about the summons?
items.lookFor: The irony that the sightless man is the only one who understands the signs and leads the way, while the sighted elders and Theseus are afraid or uncertain.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The irony is that the blind man sees most clearly. The elders are terrified, “My spirit quails and cowers” (line 1520), and Theseus is unsure whether this is “a thunderbolt of Zeus or sleet / Of arrowy hail” (lines 1552–1553), but Oedipus says, “I know full well” (line 1528). The irony shows that in this play understanding comes from the gods, not from the eyes.

items.text: In the passage that opens with “Ills on ills!”, why might Sophocles have chosen these particular words? Pick two and explain their connotations.
items.lookFor: Two words from the elders’ opening (lines 1502–1511) with their connotations, such as “Ills on ills,” “sightless guest,” “never sleeping eye” or “Overthrowing,” showing fear and a sense of fate at work.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The elders cry “Ills on ills!” (line 1502), which piles one trouble on another, and picture “Time with never sleeping eye” (line 1508), a watcher that never rests. The words show fear, but also a sense that the gods are at work: time is overthrowing the great and “Raising now from low estate” (line 1511), which may describe the guest himself.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “Thunder scene (lines 1502–1605)”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: The turn is the arrival of the god’s sign, which changes Oedipus from a man who stays to a man who leads; the effect is that he prepares to keep his promise and walk toward his end.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The turn is the arrival of the sign itself, the peals that Oedipus reads as the god calling him: “This winged thunder of the god must bear me / Anon to Hades” (lines 1516–1517). Its effect is immediate: Oedipus sends for Theseus to keep his promise, then sets out to lead the way to the place where he “must end” (line 1571).

items.text: How does “Thunder scene (lines 1502–1605)” build on “Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501)”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A causal link: having cursed his son and kept nothing back from Thebes, Oedipus now gives everything to Athens, and the elders’ sense of “Ills on ills” follows straight from the curse they have just heard.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The elders begin, “Ills on ills! no pause or rest! / Come they from our sightless guest?” (lines 1502–1503), because they have just heard him curse his son. Episode 4 showed what Oedipus withholds from those who wronged him; this scene shows what he gives to those who sheltered him, “a treasure age cannot corrupt” (line 1569).

items.text: In “Thunder scene (lines 1502–1605)”, what can we infer about a character's motives from what they say on stage about the summons, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: A motive behind his words: Oedipus could keep his last moments for his daughters, but he wants Theseus first, which shows that keeping his promise to his host matters most to him.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Oedipus loves his daughters, “though I love them dearly” (line 1579), yet his urgent concern is Theseus: “Is the prince coming?” (line 1538). His motive is to keep his word: “I would do all / I promised thee and thine before I die” (lines 1558–1559). Paying his debt to his host matters more to him than a private farewell.

items.text: Go back to the bell-ringer question (What does it mean to face the end of something calmly?). Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised answer to the bell-ringer (facing the end calmly), using Oedipus’s certainty and his care for others as he goes, set against the elders’ fear.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: I first said facing the end calmly means not caring. Oedipus shows the opposite. He is calm because he is sure, “I know full well” (line 1528), and he spends his last strength on others, blessing his host: “Blessing on thee, dearest friend, / On thee and on thy land and followers!” (lines 1602–1603). Calm here comes from purpose and gratitude, not indifference.

items.text: Where does characterization appear in “Thunder scene (lines 1502–1605)”, and how does it connect the summons to the larger concern with death and blessing?
items.lookFor: Where characterization connects the summons to death and blessing: Oedipus, at the edge of death, becomes a giver of blessing, a protector of Athens and a leader.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Facing death, Oedipus is no longer a beggar asking for help but a giver: he will “Unfold a treasure age cannot corrupt” (line 1569), a secret that will “ever serve thee for defense” (line 1574). The characterization ties his death to blessing, which matches the promise in the Prologue that he would be “A blessing to the land wherein thou dwell’st” (line 92).

items.text: Open question: is Oedipus' passing a reward, a mystery, or both? Defend any position.
items.lookFor: A defended position: a reward (honoured by the gods, a blessing for Athens) and a mystery (kept secret, without witnesses), with a counterpoint, based only on what the scene shows before the end is reported.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: both, as far as this scene shows. It feels like a reward because the gods themselves call him, “The gods themselves are heralds of my fate” (line 1561), and his grave will protect Athens. It is also a mystery: “those dread mysteries speech may not profane” (line 1576) will be known only to Theseus. Counter-line: a reader could argue that it is simply a death, and that the play hides it in religious awe. A strong answer explains why secrecy matters.

items.text: Consider this reading of the scene (a claim, not a line from the text): Oedipus recognises the peals as the gods' appointed warning and sends for Theseus while he can still speak the charge. How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the scene.
items.lookFor: A stand with two lines from the scene, with a qualification that his calm is not only acceptance but authority: he gives orders and a charge, not only a farewell.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: agree, and extend it. He recognises the warning, “Of their appointed warnings nothing fails” (line 1562), and sends for Theseus at once (lines 1513–1514). But he does more than speak a charge. He takes command and leads the way: “Let us set forth nor longer hesitate” (line 1591). The scene shows his authority as well as his acceptance.

items.text: Which character in “Thunder scene (lines 1502–1605)” acts most wisely in the matter of the summons, and which least? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: A named standard applied to two characters, for example meeting the god’s sign with understanding rather than fear, comparing Oedipus and the elders (or Theseus), with lines.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: by the standard of meeting the god’s sign with understanding, Oedipus acts most wisely: “I know full well” (line 1528). By the same standard the elders act least wisely, crying “Dread powers of air! Save, Zeus, O save!” (line 1524). A student could defend the elders: their fear is honest, and they pray for grace even toward “a man of sin” (line 1535). Theseus could also be ranked high, since he trusts a proven prophet (lines 1566–1567).

items.text: You are directing “Thunder scene (lines 1502–1605)”. Make two staging choices (a line delivery, a movement, a light or sound cue) and explain how each shapes the audience's view of the summons.
items.lookFor: Two staging choices tied to lines, such as the blind man walking unaided as the others follow, or a light cue for “O light, no light to me,” each with its effect.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: (1) On “Follow me, daughters, this way” (line 1592), let Oedipus stand and walk steadily without a hand on him while Antigone and Ismene follow, reversing every earlier entrance. (2) On “O light, no light to me, but mine erewhile” (line 1599), let a single shaft of light fall on his face, then fade as he leaves. The audience sees him lead with certainty and feels the solemn farewell.

items.text: Write your own questions about “Thunder scene (lines 1502–1605)”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions answerable from lines 1502–1605: one recall, one why/how and one should/what-if, different in kind.
followUps: Which of your questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Model set. Recall: Who alone may know the spot? (Theseus, who will pass it on only to his chosen heir, lines 1580–1582.) Why/how: Why must the place be kept secret? (It will defend Athens better than “native shields and near allies,” line 1575.) Should/what if: Should Oedipus have told his daughters the secret? (Answers weigh his love for them, line 1579, against his promise to Athens.)

items.text: Connect “Thunder scene (lines 1502–1605)”, with its focus on the summons, to refuge and hospitality: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Sophocles need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment about refuge and hospitality, the question’s theme. The link is strong: the guest repays his host with a gift that will protect the city; a strong answer says what must still be shown.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: the link is strong. Hospitality comes back as a gift: the elders call it “Thy due guerdon” for the host (line 1549), and Oedipus says the secret will “serve thee for defense / Better than native shields and near allies” (lines 1574–1575). The guest who came asking for refuge leaves his host a protection. To strengthen the link, Sophocles must show whether the promised blessing is fulfilled and how Athens keeps faith with its guest at the end.

items.text: Is the plot in “Thunder scene (lines 1502–1605)” effective in presenting the summons, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: A judgment against a stated criterion (does the plot build suspense and meaning, or does the repetition of peals feel mechanical?), with a line that meets it and one that might miss it.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: effective, because each peal raises the pressure. The elders’ terror builds (“Hark! with louder, nearer roar,” line 1518), while Oedipus asks whether Theseus will find him “living and my senses clear” (line 1539), which creates a race against time. Counter-line: a modern reader may find the repeated cries to Zeus and the warning about the “dread Dragon’s brood” (line 1584) heavy-handed. A strong answer judges whether the repetition builds dread or slows the scene.

items.text: Compare how “Thunder scene (lines 1502–1605)” treats the summons with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Oedipus at Colonus see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A named comparison (another text or film where a dying person passes on a secret or blessing, or is called by a sign) and one thing the scene sees that the other misses, tied to a line.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Compare scenes in films where a dying mentor passes on a secret to a student. This scene sees something those often miss: the secret is a gift to a whole city, not only to one person, and it must be passed “from heir to heir” (line 1582) and kept quiet to keep its power. It also shows the giver as a man who was once rejected, so the gift becomes a reversal of his whole story.

items.text: Predict what “Stasimon 4 (lines 1606–1625)” will bring, using two clues from this scene. After reading, evaluate your prediction.
items.lookFor: A prediction from two clues, Oedipus leading the way to his appointed place and his blessing on Theseus, about what the elders will sing while they wait, checked after reading.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Clue 1: Oedipus leaves saying he draws “near the final gloom / Of Hades” (lines 1601–1602). Clue 2: he blesses Theseus and his land (lines 1602–1603). The elders, left behind, will probably pray for him as he goes toward the end, and perhaps ask the powers of the dead to treat him gently. After reading, students check how the elders’ attitude to their guest has changed.

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of “Thunder scene (lines 1502–1605)” (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about the summons?
items.lookFor: An adaptation that keeps the core: a dying, once-rejected guest recognises the sign he was promised, calls for his host and leads him to a secret that will protect the host’s community. It names two details that must stay.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: An old refugee, once refused everywhere, hears the storm he was told would mark his last day and calls for the mayor who took him in. He leads the mayor alone to a place only the mayor may know and gives him what will protect the town. Two things must stay: the blind man leading the sighted (lines 1592–1593), and the secret handed only to the host (lines 1580–1582).
